Hello everyone, this is Best Shot, I’m Da Fei. 1.2 gigawatts—that is the power scale of Stargate Abilene, the AI data center in Texas built specifically for OpenAI. Since its completion, it has become the benchmark for the speed of AI infrastructure development in the U.S. But few people know that in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China, there is a campus of similar scale that is faster and costs only one-fifth as much. The first phase was just delivered this August. Our team visited the site this September and returned to write an in-depth research report. This report breaks down. in great detail how Chinese data centers are built, why they are so fast, and the power and cooling architecture behind them. Today, we’ll share it with you. First, let’s talk about the reference point, Abilene. It was developed by Crusoe Energy and operated by Oracle, nominally built for OpenAI. It features eight buildings with a total power of 1.2 gigawatts, which converts to an IT load of about 820 megawatts, taking over a year to complete. Yet during that same period, anti-data center sentiment in Texas surged. Residents protested rising electricity prices, companies complained. about grid strain, and organizations questioned resource consumption. You could say Abilene rose amidst controversy. On the Chinese side, the Galaxy campus is planned for an 800- megawatt IT load, nearly identical to Abilene, but the first 120-megawatt phase was delivered in under 12 months. The cost is roughly one-fifth of its U.S. counterpart. All four phases are custom-built for two internet giants, with full completion expected by the end of 2027. Interestingly, if the nearby wind turbine plant can be vacated later , Galaxy has room to expand to about one gigawatt. For comparison, Crusoe has. also planned expansions for Abilene, and with "behind-the-meter" capacity increases, the entire campus could eventually reach 1.5 gigawatts of IT capacity. Currently, in the Chahar High-Tech Zone surrounding the Galaxy campus, there are 22 data center projects running simultaneously, with nearly 30,000 construction workers on site. The report contains a complete breakdown of the Galaxy construction process, which is the most valuable content in the paid section. Let's walk through it. Where does the entire process begin? First, you must sign an investment agreement, then pass the power supply review by the NDRC; this is the most critical step. Any project consuming more than 10,000 tons of. standard coal—that is, exceeding 10 megawatts—cannot legally begin without passing this stage. After the start of 2025, large-scale projects also require window guidance from the NDRC. These two reviews run in parallel; adding land purchase and construction permits, it takes about four months in total. Only then does construction begin. You might think that for a building as large as a data center, just topping out would take several months. However, it only took eight to ten weeks for the first Galaxy building to go from groundbreaking to topping out. Why is it so fast? Because the soil conditions in Ulanqab are favorable, allowing for spread footing technology without piling. The foundation was finished in a month, and. the concrete frame above was built at a rate of one floor per week, taking another month. So, the first Galaxy building was topped out by the end of October, just in time before winter arrived in Inner Mongolia. Subsequent work moved indoors, and using precast concrete panels instead of bricks for exterior and partition walls saved a lot of time. After the winter equipment orders were confirmed, MEP fit-out—that is, mechanical and electrical piping and electrical wiring—was all started directly indoors. Then, there is the data that best reflects "China Speed": the peak construction workforce. For a 100 to 120-megawatt data center, Galaxy had 3,000 to 4,000 people working.

simultaneously during the peak MEP fit-out phase. The report compares this with similar projects in the U.S., where the peak is only about 800 to 1,300 people, a three-to five-fold difference . After the project is delivered, the construction team moves on to the next data center, usually in another park, while the operations team stays behind. Every 100 acres of land can create about 100 local jobs. Another difference between China and the U.S. worth mentioning is that in China, data centers are usually delivered as turnkey solutions; developers install everything , including racks, power distribution, and cooling systems, so tenants only need to bring in their servers and. cables. In the U.S., it is more common to have "powered shell" delivery, where the developer provides an energized empty shell, and tenants handle their own internal power and cooling design. Alright, we've covered the speed; now let's answer another question: why are costs so low? The report provides three reasons. The first is supply chain localization. In 2021, about half of the equipment in Chinese data centers was imported. Now, 80%to 90%is domestic, including products manufactured in China by international brands like Schneider, ABB, and Siemens; for example, UPS systems are almost entirely localized. Currently, the main items still requiring imports are HVAC compressors, fans, and main circuit breakers. Although diesel generators are still primarily imported, domestic brands are on the rise because the lead times from overseas suppliers have become too long . The second reason is an increase in IT utilization, which is quite counterintuitive. In a campus with 100 megawatts of grid access, you can't just allocate all 100 megawatts to servers. A portion goes to cooling, some is lost in transformers and substations, plus there’s lighting and office power. The part actually reserved for racks is designed based on the peak load during. the hottest afternoon of the year, not the annual average PUE. Traditionally, 100 megawatts of grid access corresponds to about 67 to 68 megawatts of critical IT load. Now, this number has increased to 70 to 72 megawatts, and the extra percentage points come from three changes. First, cooling systems rely more on outdoor air and higher water temperatures. Second, power distribution architecture reduces conversion steps. Third, equipment capacity is selected based on actual measured server power, not nameplate capacity, typically targeting a 70%to 80%load rate. Since the costs for substations and main. transformers are calculated based on grid connection scale, the same cost now supports more IT volume, bringing the unit cost down. The third reason, though not explicitly stated in the report, is something everyone can probably guess: construction costs themselves are much lower than in the U.S. Now, let's look at power from a different perspective, which is the most noteworthy aspect of Galaxy. Galaxy uses a model that China has been promoting in recent years called "source-grid-load-storage." Simply put, the project builds its own wind power, energy storage, and data centers, connecting them all with dedicated lines and bypassing the public. grid entirely. The benefit is direct: electricity prices remain fixed long-term, unaffected by grid fluctuations, and the wind power counts toward green energy targets. In Ulanqab , the wind is particularly strong, with a capacity factor of 35%to 40%, which is even better than the Inner Mongolia average of 32%. The group built two wind farms near the campus, about 80 kilometers apart, ensuring complementary wind conditions; when one isn't spinning , the other is likely still running. The two wind farms have a combined installed capacity of 420 megawatts, while the data center's second phase has a total load of 240 megawatts. The wind capacity is 1.75 times the load. Paired with a 4.

-hour energy storage system, the goal is for over 60%of the power for the first two phases to come from their own wind farms. Regarding how to calculate the wind power ratio in the grid, B has a very clear model. If wind power capacity and load are at a 1-to-1 ratio, under good wind conditions, wind power can cover about 40%of annual electricity consumption. By doubling the wind power , even when wind speeds are relatively low, it can cover a significant amount of load, raising the wind power ratio to over 55%. Adding energy storage allows the excess power generated during high winds to be saved for use when the wind dies down. Of course, energy storage is not a cure-all, so when there is no wind. for several consecutive days, we still have to rely on the power grid. Certainly, Envision Group is doing much more at Galaxy than just building a wind farm. This company is an established wind power developer that has installed over 100 gigawatts of turbines globally , but in the Galaxy project, it plays three roles simultaneously. The first layer is the traditional developer and operator, which is nothing unusual. The second layer is the equipment manufacturer, including the full wind turbine units, converters, and control software, all of which are self-developed. The batteries come from its affiliate, Envision AESC. From the battery cells to the energy storage system, power conversion system, and PCS software, everything is self-developed. They can be fully assembled and tested in the factory, then transported to the site and plugged in. The traditional approach involves different vendors bringing various components to the site for individual commissioning, a process that takes anywhere from three months to over half a year. However, Envision Group's factory pre-configuration model has reduced on-site commissioning to under three months. The third role is as a substation system integrator, which is the most interesting part. The Galaxy park has a 5-megawatt server room powered by 800-volt DC. How is this achieved? They used a device called a Solid-State Transformer (SST) to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage AC directly. into 800-volt DC for the server racks, bypassing the entire set of traditional equipment like step-down transformers, UPS, and rectifiers. Beyond that, Envision Group also co-designed the prefabricated substations in the park. These substations are built and tested in modular form at the factory while on-site construction is still underway, and afterward, they are just transported and connected. A traditional indoor substation takes about six months from start of construction to power connection, while Envision’s approach can cut this down to under three months . Galaxy is Envision's first project in Inner Mongolia, and its total planned capacity there adds up to 3 gigawatts. Why is this worth discussing separately ? Because the global data center power supply architecture is currently at a turning point, and China and the United States are following two completely different evolutionary paths. Let's first clarify the context. A previous in-depth report by SMAnalysis in the US outlined a four-stage path, starting from rack-level conversion and gradually progressing to building-wide DC, eventually reaching the substation level by converting medium-voltage AC directly into 800V DC. Rack-level set means converting on-site right next to the racks, while building-wide DC means electrifying the entire building. China , however, skipped several of these. early stages and began using DC in data centers back in 2007. How exactly did this happen? Because China's data center industry originated from telecommunications. It developed from telecom carriers, whose telecom networks ......have been running on 48V DC from the very beginning. In 2007, China Telecom's Jiangsu branch began piloting 240V DC. Replacing UPS with DC improved efficiency by 3%to 4%. Choosing 240V made sense because it falls within the input range of standard server power supplies, allowing you to just swap the UPS for a rectifier without touching the servers themselves. China Mobile tested a 336V alternative in 2012, but that.

required dedicated server power supplies , so it saw less widespread adoption. After that, hyperscale customers caught on, and many new data centers adopted a dual-power supply setup combining 240V DC and utility power. However, it is still far from universal, as the UPS remains the...Ali......Baba went even further. Their engineers asked a question: between the 10kV power grid and the servers, why do we need separate transformers, switchgear, and rectifiers ? And so, the "Pama" power system was born. The name is taken from "Pama," meaning to dig through and connect all the intermediate links. Pama integrates. 10kV power distribution, a transformer, modular rectifiers, and output distribution into a single prefabricated unit, converting 10kV AC directly into 240V DC. The Pama power system began testing in 2018 and has now become the standard configuration for Alibaba Cloud's self-built data centers. According to Alibaba Cloud's ESG report , by March 2023, there were 366 Pama units installed, totaling over 800 MW. Data from the industry is even more aggressive; by August 2024, Pama had over 500 units installed across Alibaba and other operators, with a total installed capacity exceeding 1 GW. In. terms of efficiency, the rectifier module's peak efficiency is 98.5%, with an overall system efficiency of about 97.5%. It occupies only half the space of traditional designs, with equipment and construction work reduced by 40%. Alright, now let's talk about the Galaxy vision. It takes this path a step further, adopting 800V DC instead of 240V, and actually delivering it all the way to the rack. ST replaces traditional transformers and rectifiers with power electronics, boosting output voltage from 240V to 800V. According to data from the CHINT Group, efficiency exceeds 98.5%, and the footprint is cut in half. . Many other ST projects convert back to 240V before the rack, but not Galaxy; it keeps 800V DC running to the rack, where a DC-DC converter steps it down. This sounds simple, but mature rack-side components are designed for low or medium-low voltages, making 800V a new frontier. This 5MW server room has three 1000V outputs: two follow traditional AC and low-voltage DC paths, while the third uses the ST 800V DC bus, which also connects to a BSS battery energy. storage system. The server rack connects to all three, so the conventional path remains, allowing the 800V path to be tested safely. Beyond the hardware challenges, system coordination is another major hurdle. With AC, low-voltage DC, 800V DC, and batteries involved, the system must detect voltage drops in seconds: which path failed, should ST adjust current, or should the battery discharge? Galaxy uses a proprietary control system developed in-house by the CHINT Group to handle this. The third-party LIS provides a broader observation: US data center. power upgrades are driven by racks, like NVIDIA’s GB200 rack hitting 600kW. At this density, traditional voltage efficiency becomes an issue, necessitating a shift to 800V, whereas in China, where DC infrastructure exists , everyone is moving toward 800V and SST regardless of rack power. It is fair to say these two paths chose different starting points, but they are heading toward the same destination. Speaking of BSS, here are three reasons why battery energy storage is becoming increasingly important in data centers. First is green power; projects relying on wind and solar use storage to bridge renewables and the grid. Second is the.

grid itself; AI training loads fluctuate wildly as thousands of GPUs switch on and off, sending shockwaves to the grid . Grid operators in China are now imposing increasingly strict low-voltage ride-through requirements on large data centers. The third is backup. Once the UPS is removed, the rack-level battery BBU can only last about 90 seconds, while the BSS can carry the load until the diesel generators start. Data centers powered by the grid now typically include 30 minutes to an hour of energy storage, and some buyers have started requesting even longer durations . Power is mostly covered. The final. core module is cooling. The report states that this design was one of the most impressive parts of the entire project because it directly addresses a debate currently happening in the U.S. data center industry. To set the background: Jensen Huang said at CES 2026, "GPU systems can be cooled with 45 ° C water; there's no need for chillers ." This statement sparked significant discussion within the industry. Server hardware can indeed handle 45 ° C water , but in reality, most data centers still retain centralized chillers. Why? Because cold plates only cool the main. chips; other parts of the server, such as cards other than the CPU, networking gear, and storage devices, still rely on air cooling. In most designs, the air-cooled fan walls and the liquid-cooled Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) share the same water loop. The liquid-cooling side works fine with 45 ° C water, but fan walls require water temperatures around 25 ° C to achieve similar heat exchange efficiency. Therefore, the centralized chiller must cool the entire loop to 25 ° C, which means the thermal headroom on the liquid-cooling side is wasted. Some might ask, why not just split the loop. into two? One line for warm water to handle liquid cooling, and one for cold water for air cooling. The problem is that it’s uncertain how much air cooling versus liquid cooling a tenant will need in the future when the facility is being built. If you split them into two fixed loops, it's very difficult for the data center to adjust once tenant needs differ from the original design. For developers making 15-year long-term investments, flexibility is more important than marginal efficiency gains , so most still choose to share the loop and keep the centralized chillers. However, the Galaxy design provides an interesting answer to this trade-off: it still shares a single water loop, but without centralized chillers. The first. phase of Galaxy delivered 30 MW of liquid cooling capacity. The liquid-cooling side is designed to handle the majority of the heat, while the air-cooling side is designed to handle up to 50%. Since the two numbers add up to over 100%, it means the ratio can be adjusted flexibly. If today's tenant wants more liquid-cooled racks, fine; if a tenant tomorrow needs more air-cooled equipment, that's fine too. So, how is that actually achieved? On the cooling side, it's pretty similar to what we see in the US. The cold plate sits on the chip, the CDU moves the heat into the facility water loop, and the loop carries the hot water to the roof. In this loop, the water outlet temperature reaches 35 ° C in summer,. and the return is 43 ° C. For most of the year in Lanchabu, the ambient air temperature is below 43 ° C, so the dry cooler on the roof can cool the water down on its own, with no need for a chiller. The key to the air-cooled side is that each fan wall contains two heat exchange coils; the air first passes through a water coil connected to the roof’s water loop, and in winter, the return water from the roof is cool enough to bring the air down to 25 ° C. But that doesn't work in summer, as the water temperature won't drop low enough , so each fan wall also has an internal compressor coil that only runs during the hottest days. The power capacity of.

this compressor coil is designed for the hottest day of the year, so it doesn't need to run around the clock. Comparing the fan wall with an integrated compressor coil to installing a magnetic bearing chiller on the roof, the former saves 10%to 20%, and since that chiller is actually a dry cooler, it sits idle most of the year; given Lanchabu’s annual average temperature is around 4 ° C, you get nearly 10 months of free cooling, so keeping a chiller is just a waste of money. So, can this design be used in warmer regions? For example, in Texas, the answer is yes. However, the compressor coils would need to run longer, so you wouldn't save as much. money. This design’s advantages are greatest in cooler climates. That’s about it for the Galaxy story; finally, let’s look at the bigger picture. Vertical integration is the core keyword for Galaxy—from servers to energy storage, from 10kV power to 800V DC racks, and from substations to cooling design, the Envision Group acted as manufacturer, designer, and integrator for this project. This isn't the only company in China doing this; another more widely known case is the partnership between VNET, CATL, and Zhongheng Electric. VNET is a leading global colocation operator, and needless. to say, CATL became VNET’s largest shareholder in 2024 and simultaneously announced the acquisition of shares from Zhongheng Electric’s controlling shareholder. Zhongheng Electric is a major supplier of HVDC systems for Alibaba Cloud and ByteDance data centers ; together, the three link up data center operations, green power storage, and in-rack power supply. CATL is also one of the largest external investors in DeepRoute.ai, which means they have already taken a step toward the model side. Jing Group handles most links internally, while CAT connects various companies through partnerships and equity. Though the paths differ, the. logic is the same: in a highly competitive market, you must control more links in the value chain. Data center rents in China have been cut in half over five years, CAPEX has dropped by 25%, and electricity prices in Inner Mongolia are among the lowest in the world. In this environment, vertical integration is a very natural strategy for differentiation. Of course, it is hard to say yet whether vertical integration can become a true competitive advantage. Currently, hyperscale cloud providers primarily choose suppliers based on resource abundance and past performance, but two trends are worth noting. First, securing electricity is becoming a core competency for data center developers. The U.S. relies on gas turbines and fuel cells to bridge grid gaps, Malaysia now requires data centers to source at least 30%of their power from renewables, and under China’s "East Data, West Computing " policy, projects near energy sources get priority approval. Second, the redesign of rack power architectures is underway, and the roadmap has not been set in stone yet. Players capable of providing an integrated package of energy and power distribution infrastructure will increasingly widen their competitive lead over those who only build data center shells. So, do you think China's data center construction speed and cost advantages can be replicated in the U.S.? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments section.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 比較德州 Stargate Abilene 與內蒙古「銀河」園區，呈現中美大型 AI 資料中心在建設速度、規模與交付方式上的差異。
  • 拆解銀河園區如何縮短工期，從審批、地基施工到機電裝修，了解「中國速度」背後的具體做法。
  • 說明資料中心成本下降的原因，包括供應鏈在地化、提高 IT 負載利用率，以及較低的施工成本。
  • 深入介紹「源網荷儲」與風電、儲能的配置，並說明能源智造集團如何整合開發、設備製造和系統整合。

摘要

兩座大型 AI 資料中心的比較

大飛以德州 Stargate Abilene 作為參照。這座由 Crusoe Energy 開發、Oracle 營運、名義上為 OpenAI 建設的園區，包含八棟建築，總電力規模達1.2 吉瓦，換算 IT 負載約 820 兆瓦，建設超過一年，期間也引發當地居民對電價上漲、電網負荷和資源消耗的疑慮。

相較之下，內蒙古烏蘭察布的「銀河」園區規劃 IT 負載 800 兆瓦，規模與 Abilene 接近；首期 120 兆瓦卻在不到 12 個月內交付，成本約為美國同類項目的五分之一。園區分四期建設，預計 2027 年底完成；若未來騰出鄰近風機工廠用地，還有機會擴至約 1 吉瓦。當地察哈爾高新區也有 22 個資料中心項目同步施工，現場施工人員近三萬人。

快速施工的流程與做法

大型資料中心動工前，須先簽訂投資協議並通過發改委的電力供應審查；用能超過一萬噸標準煤、也就是超過 10 兆瓦的項目，依法不能跳過這道關卡。自 2025 年起，大型項目還須接受發改委窗口指導。相關審查與土地、施工許可等程序並行處理，整體約需四個月。

銀河首棟建築從動土到封頂僅花八至十週。當地土質適合採用擴展基礎，不必打樁，地基約一個月完成；混凝土結構則以每週一層的速度施工，再用一個月左右封頂，趕在內蒙古入冬前完成主體。後續室內工程改用預製混凝土板作為外牆與隔間，並在設備訂單確認後直接進行機電管線和電氣配線施工。

在 100 至 120 兆瓦規模的資料中心中，銀河機電裝修高峰期同時投入約 3,000 至 4,000 名工人；報告比較的美國同類項目則約有 800 至 1,300 人。大飛指出，工程交付後，施工團隊通常轉往其他園區，營運團隊則留下；每百英畝土地約可創造 100 個在地職缺。交付方式也有差異：中國常由開發商提供包含機櫃、配電與冷卻系統的交鑰匙方案，美國則較常交付已有電力、但內部設備仍待租戶配置的「動力空殼」。

成本較低的三項原因

報告提出的第一個原因是供應鏈在地化。2021 年中國資料中心設備約有一半仰賴進口，如今國產或在中國製造的比例已達八至九成，UPS 等設備尤其如此。仍較常需要進口的項目包括空調壓縮機、風機和主斷路器；柴油發電機也仍以進口為主，但本土品牌逐漸增加，部分原因是海外交貨期拉長。

第二個原因是 IT 負載利用率提高。過去每 100 兆瓦電網接入容量，約能配置 67 至 68 兆瓦關鍵 IT 負載；如今已提高到約 70 至 72 兆瓦。這來自更多利用室外空氣與較高水溫進行冷卻、減少配電轉換環節，以及依伺服器實際功率而非銘牌容量配置設備。由於變電站和主變壓器成本按接入電力規模計算，同樣的電力基礎設施能支撐更多 IT 負載，單位成本因而下降。第三個原因則是中國的施工成本本身較低。

風電、儲能與「源網荷儲」

銀河園區採用中國近年推動的「源網荷儲」模式：自行建設風電與儲能，再透過專線連接資料中心，盡量不依賴公共電網。這可讓電價長期保持穩定，也有助於達成綠電目標。烏蘭察布風力條件佳，容量因數約 35% 至 40%；園區在相距約 80 公里的地點建設兩座風場，利用風況互補，合計裝置容量 420 兆瓦。銀河二期負載為 240 兆瓦，風電裝置容量約為負載的 1.75 倍，並搭配四小時儲能，目標是讓前兩期超過六成的用電來自自建風場。

大飛說明，風電容量與負載若按一比一配置，在風況良好時約可供應全年四成用電；增加風電容量，即使風勢較弱，也能提高綠電占比至五成五以上。儲能則可保存強風時的多餘電力，留待風勢減弱時使用，但若連續多日無風，仍須仰賴電網。

能源智造集團的整合角色

能源智造集團在銀河項目中同時扮演多重角色：除了風電開發商與營運商，也是風機、變流器及控制軟體的設備製造商；儲能電池則由旗下企業提供，從電芯、儲能系統到電力轉換系統及軟體皆自行開發。設備能在工廠預先組裝與測試，運抵現場後即可接入，將傳統多家廠商分別進場、耗時三個月至半年以上的調試流程，縮短至三個月內。

影片最後轉向變電站系統整合，提到銀河園區有一間採用800 伏特直流電供電的 5 兆瓦伺服器機房，並介紹固態變壓器可將 10 千伏交流電直接轉換為伺服器機櫃所需的 800 伏特直流電。字幕在此處中斷，未進一步交代其後續架構。

================================================

Hello everyone, this is Best Shot, I’m Da Fei. 1.2 gigawatts—that is the power scale of Stargate Abilene, the AI data center in Texas built specifically for OpenAI. Since its completion, it has become the benchmark for the speed of AI infrastructure development in the U.S. But few people know that in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, China, there is a campus of similar scale that is faster and costs only one-fifth as much. The first phase was just delivered this August. Our team visited the site this September and returned to write an in-depth research report. This report breaks down. in great detail how Chinese data centers are built, why they are so fast, and the power and cooling architecture behind them. Today, we’ll share it with you. First, let’s talk about the reference point, Abilene. It was developed by Crusoe Energy and operated by Oracle, nominally built for OpenAI. It features eight buildings with a total power of 1.2 gigawatts, which converts to an IT load of about 820 megawatts, taking over a year to complete. Yet during that same period, anti-data center sentiment in Texas surged. Residents protested rising electricity prices, companies complained. about grid strain, and organizations questioned resource consumption. You could say Abilene rose amidst controversy. On the Chinese side, the Galaxy campus is planned for an 800- megawatt IT load, nearly identical to Abilene, but the first 120-megawatt phase was delivered in under 12 months. The cost is roughly one-fifth of its U.S. counterpart. All four phases are custom-built for two internet giants, with full completion expected by the end of 2027. Interestingly, if the nearby wind turbine plant can be vacated later , Galaxy has room to expand to about one gigawatt. For comparison, Crusoe has. also planned expansions for Abilene, and with "behind-the-meter" capacity increases, the entire campus could eventually reach 1.5 gigawatts of IT capacity. Currently, in the Chahar High-Tech Zone surrounding the Galaxy campus, there are 22 data center projects running simultaneously, with nearly 30,000 construction workers on site. The report contains a complete breakdown of the Galaxy construction process, which is the most valuable content in the paid section. Let's walk through it. Where does the entire process begin? First, you must sign an investment agreement, then pass the power supply review by the NDRC; this is the most critical step. Any project consuming more than 10,000 tons of. standard coal—that is, exceeding 10 megawatts—cannot legally begin without passing this stage. After the start of 2025, large-scale projects also require window guidance from the NDRC. These two reviews run in parallel; adding land purchase and construction permits, it takes about four months in total. Only then does construction begin. You might think that for a building as large as a data center, just topping out would take several months. However, it only took eight to ten weeks for the first Galaxy building to go from groundbreaking to topping out. Why is it so fast? Because the soil conditions in Ulanqab are favorable, allowing for spread footing technology without piling. The foundation was finished in a month, and. the concrete frame above was built at a rate of one floor per week, taking another month. So, the first Galaxy building was topped out by the end of October, just in time before winter arrived in Inner Mongolia. Subsequent work moved indoors, and using precast concrete panels instead of bricks for exterior and partition walls saved a lot of time. After the winter equipment orders were confirmed, MEP fit-out—that is, mechanical and electrical piping and electrical wiring—was all started directly indoors. Then, there is the data that best reflects "China Speed": the peak construction workforce. For a 100 to 120-megawatt data center, Galaxy had 3,000 to 4,000 people working.

simultaneously during the peak MEP fit-out phase. The report compares this with similar projects in the U.S., where the peak is only about 800 to 1,300 people, a three-to five-fold difference . After the project is delivered, the construction team moves on to the next data center, usually in another park, while the operations team stays behind. Every 100 acres of land can create about 100 local jobs. Another difference between China and the U.S. worth mentioning is that in China, data centers are usually delivered as turnkey solutions; developers install everything , including racks, power distribution, and cooling systems, so tenants only need to bring in their servers and. cables. In the U.S., it is more common to have "powered shell" delivery, where the developer provides an energized empty shell, and tenants handle their own internal power and cooling design. Alright, we've covered the speed; now let's answer another question: why are costs so low? The report provides three reasons. The first is supply chain localization. In 2021, about half of the equipment in Chinese data centers was imported. Now, 80%to 90%is domestic, including products manufactured in China by international brands like Schneider, ABB, and Siemens; for example, UPS systems are almost entirely localized. Currently, the main items still requiring imports are HVAC compressors, fans, and main circuit breakers. Although diesel generators are still primarily imported, domestic brands are on the rise because the lead times from overseas suppliers have become too long . The second reason is an increase in IT utilization, which is quite counterintuitive. In a campus with 100 megawatts of grid access, you can't just allocate all 100 megawatts to servers. A portion goes to cooling, some is lost in transformers and substations, plus there’s lighting and office power. The part actually reserved for racks is designed based on the peak load during. the hottest afternoon of the year, not the annual average PUE. Traditionally, 100 megawatts of grid access corresponds to about 67 to 68 megawatts of critical IT load. Now, this number has increased to 70 to 72 megawatts, and the extra percentage points come from three changes. First, cooling systems rely more on outdoor air and higher water temperatures. Second, power distribution architecture reduces conversion steps. Third, equipment capacity is selected based on actual measured server power, not nameplate capacity, typically targeting a 70%to 80%load rate. Since the costs for substations and main. transformers are calculated based on grid connection scale, the same cost now supports more IT volume, bringing the unit cost down. The third reason, though not explicitly stated in the report, is something everyone can probably guess: construction costs themselves are much lower than in the U.S. Now, let's look at power from a different perspective, which is the most noteworthy aspect of Galaxy. Galaxy uses a model that China has been promoting in recent years called "source-grid-load-storage." Simply put, the project builds its own wind power, energy storage, and data centers, connecting them all with dedicated lines and bypassing the public. grid entirely. The benefit is direct: electricity prices remain fixed long-term, unaffected by grid fluctuations, and the wind power counts toward green energy targets. In Ulanqab , the wind is particularly strong, with a capacity factor of 35%to 40%, which is even better than the Inner Mongolia average of 32%. The group built two wind farms near the campus, about 80 kilometers apart, ensuring complementary wind conditions; when one isn't spinning , the other is likely still running. The two wind farms have a combined installed capacity of 420 megawatts, while the data center's second phase has a total load of 240 megawatts. The wind capacity is 1.75 times the load. Paired with a 4.

-hour energy storage system, the goal is for over 60%of the power for the first two phases to come from their own wind farms. Regarding how to calculate the wind power ratio in the grid, B has a very clear model. If wind power capacity and load are at a 1-to-1 ratio, under good wind conditions, wind power can cover about 40%of annual electricity consumption. By doubling the wind power , even when wind speeds are relatively low, it can cover a significant amount of load, raising the wind power ratio to over 55%. Adding energy storage allows the excess power generated during high winds to be saved for use when the wind dies down. Of course, energy storage is not a cure-all, so when there is no wind. for several consecutive days, we still have to rely on the power grid. Certainly, Envision Group is doing much more at Galaxy than just building a wind farm. This company is an established wind power developer that has installed over 100 gigawatts of turbines globally , but in the Galaxy project, it plays three roles simultaneously. The first layer is the traditional developer and operator, which is nothing unusual. The second layer is the equipment manufacturer, including the full wind turbine units, converters, and control software, all of which are self-developed. The batteries come from its affiliate, Envision AESC. From the battery cells to the energy storage system, power conversion system, and PCS software, everything is self-developed. They can be fully assembled and tested in the factory, then transported to the site and plugged in. The traditional approach involves different vendors bringing various components to the site for individual commissioning, a process that takes anywhere from three months to over half a year. However, Envision Group's factory pre-configuration model has reduced on-site commissioning to under three months. The third role is as a substation system integrator, which is the most interesting part. The Galaxy park has a 5-megawatt server room powered by 800-volt DC. How is this achieved? They used a device called a Solid-State Transformer (SST) to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage AC directly. into 800-volt DC for the server racks, bypassing the entire set of traditional equipment like step-down transformers, UPS, and rectifiers. Beyond that, Envision Group also co-designed the prefabricated substations in the park. These substations are built and tested in modular form at the factory while on-site construction is still underway, and afterward, they are just transported and connected. A traditional indoor substation takes about six months from start of construction to power connection, while Envision’s approach can cut this down to under three months . Galaxy is Envision's first project in Inner Mongolia, and its total planned capacity there adds up to 3 gigawatts. Why is this worth discussing separately ? Because the global data center power supply architecture is currently at a turning point, and China and the United States are following two completely different evolutionary paths. Let's first clarify the context. A previous in-depth report by SMAnalysis in the US outlined a four-stage path, starting from rack-level conversion and gradually progressing to building-wide DC, eventually reaching the substation level by converting medium-voltage AC directly into 800V DC. Rack-level set means converting on-site right next to the racks, while building-wide DC means electrifying the entire building. China , however, skipped several of these. early stages and began using DC in data centers back in 2007. How exactly did this happen? Because China's data center industry originated from telecommunications. It developed from telecom carriers, whose telecom networks ......have been running on 48V DC from the very beginning. In 2007, China Telecom's Jiangsu branch began piloting 240V DC. Replacing UPS with DC improved efficiency by 3%to 4%. Choosing 240V made sense because it falls within the input range of standard server power supplies, allowing you to just swap the UPS for a rectifier without touching the servers themselves. China Mobile tested a 336V alternative in 2012, but that.

required dedicated server power supplies , so it saw less widespread adoption. After that, hyperscale customers caught on, and many new data centers adopted a dual-power supply setup combining 240V DC and utility power. However, it is still far from universal, as the UPS remains the...Ali......Baba went even further. Their engineers asked a question: between the 10kV power grid and the servers, why do we need separate transformers, switchgear, and rectifiers ? And so, the "Pama" power system was born. The name is taken from "Pama," meaning to dig through and connect all the intermediate links. Pama integrates. 10kV power distribution, a transformer, modular rectifiers, and output distribution into a single prefabricated unit, converting 10kV AC directly into 240V DC. The Pama power system began testing in 2018 and has now become the standard configuration for Alibaba Cloud's self-built data centers. According to Alibaba Cloud's ESG report , by March 2023, there were 366 Pama units installed, totaling over 800 MW. Data from the industry is even more aggressive; by August 2024, Pama had over 500 units installed across Alibaba and other operators, with a total installed capacity exceeding 1 GW. In. terms of efficiency, the rectifier module's peak efficiency is 98.5%, with an overall system efficiency of about 97.5%. It occupies only half the space of traditional designs, with equipment and construction work reduced by 40%. Alright, now let's talk about the Galaxy vision. It takes this path a step further, adopting 800V DC instead of 240V, and actually delivering it all the way to the rack. ST replaces traditional transformers and rectifiers with power electronics, boosting output voltage from 240V to 800V. According to data from the CHINT Group, efficiency exceeds 98.5%, and the footprint is cut in half. . Many other ST projects convert back to 240V before the rack, but not Galaxy; it keeps 800V DC running to the rack, where a DC-DC converter steps it down. This sounds simple, but mature rack-side components are designed for low or medium-low voltages, making 800V a new frontier. This 5MW server room has three 1000V outputs: two follow traditional AC and low-voltage DC paths, while the third uses the ST 800V DC bus, which also connects to a BSS battery energy. storage system. The server rack connects to all three, so the conventional path remains, allowing the 800V path to be tested safely. Beyond the hardware challenges, system coordination is another major hurdle. With AC, low-voltage DC, 800V DC, and batteries involved, the system must detect voltage drops in seconds: which path failed, should ST adjust current, or should the battery discharge? Galaxy uses a proprietary control system developed in-house by the CHINT Group to handle this. The third-party LIS provides a broader observation: US data center. power upgrades are driven by racks, like NVIDIA’s GB200 rack hitting 600kW. At this density, traditional voltage efficiency becomes an issue, necessitating a shift to 800V, whereas in China, where DC infrastructure exists , everyone is moving toward 800V and SST regardless of rack power. It is fair to say these two paths chose different starting points, but they are heading toward the same destination. Speaking of BSS, here are three reasons why battery energy storage is becoming increasingly important in data centers. First is green power; projects relying on wind and solar use storage to bridge renewables and the grid. Second is the.

grid itself; AI training loads fluctuate wildly as thousands of GPUs switch on and off, sending shockwaves to the grid . Grid operators in China are now imposing increasingly strict low-voltage ride-through requirements on large data centers. The third is backup. Once the UPS is removed, the rack-level battery BBU can only last about 90 seconds, while the BSS can carry the load until the diesel generators start. Data centers powered by the grid now typically include 30 minutes to an hour of energy storage, and some buyers have started requesting even longer durations . Power is mostly covered. The final. core module is cooling. The report states that this design was one of the most impressive parts of the entire project because it directly addresses a debate currently happening in the U.S. data center industry. To set the background: Jensen Huang said at CES 2026, "GPU systems can be cooled with 45 ° C water; there's no need for chillers ." This statement sparked significant discussion within the industry. Server hardware can indeed handle 45 ° C water , but in reality, most data centers still retain centralized chillers. Why? Because cold plates only cool the main. chips; other parts of the server, such as cards other than the CPU, networking gear, and storage devices, still rely on air cooling. In most designs, the air-cooled fan walls and the liquid-cooled Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) share the same water loop. The liquid-cooling side works fine with 45 ° C water, but fan walls require water temperatures around 25 ° C to achieve similar heat exchange efficiency. Therefore, the centralized chiller must cool the entire loop to 25 ° C, which means the thermal headroom on the liquid-cooling side is wasted. Some might ask, why not just split the loop. into two? One line for warm water to handle liquid cooling, and one for cold water for air cooling. The problem is that it’s uncertain how much air cooling versus liquid cooling a tenant will need in the future when the facility is being built. If you split them into two fixed loops, it's very difficult for the data center to adjust once tenant needs differ from the original design. For developers making 15-year long-term investments, flexibility is more important than marginal efficiency gains , so most still choose to share the loop and keep the centralized chillers. However, the Galaxy design provides an interesting answer to this trade-off: it still shares a single water loop, but without centralized chillers. The first. phase of Galaxy delivered 30 MW of liquid cooling capacity. The liquid-cooling side is designed to handle the majority of the heat, while the air-cooling side is designed to handle up to 50%. Since the two numbers add up to over 100%, it means the ratio can be adjusted flexibly. If today's tenant wants more liquid-cooled racks, fine; if a tenant tomorrow needs more air-cooled equipment, that's fine too. So, how is that actually achieved? On the cooling side, it's pretty similar to what we see in the US. The cold plate sits on the chip, the CDU moves the heat into the facility water loop, and the loop carries the hot water to the roof. In this loop, the water outlet temperature reaches 35 ° C in summer,. and the return is 43 ° C. For most of the year in Lanchabu, the ambient air temperature is below 43 ° C, so the dry cooler on the roof can cool the water down on its own, with no need for a chiller. The key to the air-cooled side is that each fan wall contains two heat exchange coils; the air first passes through a water coil connected to the roof’s water loop, and in winter, the return water from the roof is cool enough to bring the air down to 25 ° C. But that doesn't work in summer, as the water temperature won't drop low enough , so each fan wall also has an internal compressor coil that only runs during the hottest days. The power capacity of.

this compressor coil is designed for the hottest day of the year, so it doesn't need to run around the clock. Comparing the fan wall with an integrated compressor coil to installing a magnetic bearing chiller on the roof, the former saves 10%to 20%, and since that chiller is actually a dry cooler, it sits idle most of the year; given Lanchabu’s annual average temperature is around 4 ° C, you get nearly 10 months of free cooling, so keeping a chiller is just a waste of money. So, can this design be used in warmer regions? For example, in Texas, the answer is yes. However, the compressor coils would need to run longer, so you wouldn't save as much. money. This design’s advantages are greatest in cooler climates. That’s about it for the Galaxy story; finally, let’s look at the bigger picture. Vertical integration is the core keyword for Galaxy—from servers to energy storage, from 10kV power to 800V DC racks, and from substations to cooling design, the Envision Group acted as manufacturer, designer, and integrator for this project. This isn't the only company in China doing this; another more widely known case is the partnership between VNET, CATL, and Zhongheng Electric. VNET is a leading global colocation operator, and needless. to say, CATL became VNET’s largest shareholder in 2024 and simultaneously announced the acquisition of shares from Zhongheng Electric’s controlling shareholder. Zhongheng Electric is a major supplier of HVDC systems for Alibaba Cloud and ByteDance data centers ; together, the three link up data center operations, green power storage, and in-rack power supply. CATL is also one of the largest external investors in DeepRoute.ai, which means they have already taken a step toward the model side. Jing Group handles most links internally, while CAT connects various companies through partnerships and equity. Though the paths differ, the. logic is the same: in a highly competitive market, you must control more links in the value chain. Data center rents in China have been cut in half over five years, CAPEX has dropped by 25%, and electricity prices in Inner Mongolia are among the lowest in the world. In this environment, vertical integration is a very natural strategy for differentiation. Of course, it is hard to say yet whether vertical integration can become a true competitive advantage. Currently, hyperscale cloud providers primarily choose suppliers based on resource abundance and past performance, but two trends are worth noting. First, securing electricity is becoming a core competency for data center developers. The U.S. relies on gas turbines and fuel cells to bridge grid gaps, Malaysia now requires data centers to source at least 30%of their power from renewables, and under China’s "East Data, West Computing " policy, projects near energy sources get priority approval. Second, the redesign of rack power architectures is underway, and the roadmap has not been set in stone yet. Players capable of providing an integrated package of energy and power distribution infrastructure will increasingly widen their competitive lead over those who only build data center shells. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解新一代 Claude 模型如何透過多代理協作，完成複雜的數學證明與工程任務。
  • 從電路板設計、理論物理、化學到營運研究，掌握 AI 在真實專業工作中的應用成果。
  • 看見 AI 在程式開發、資安、機器人控制等領域的能力，以及它仍不均衡的限制。

摘要

新模型與自主協作能力

影片中，大飛介紹 Anthropic 的新模型 Claude 3.5 Sonnet 與 Claude 3.5 Opus，並以 AI 代理團隊證明費馬最後定理的案例揭開主題：1,000 個代理持續運作 30 小時，完成逐行可由電腦驗證的形式化證明；相較之下，先前的研究版本花了 11 天，而另一組同規模代理則在進度停滯前只完成約四分之一。這些案例顯示，模型已能自行分工、組隊並持續推進任務。

效能、價格與硬體設計

大飛指出，新模型面向最複雜的技術挑戰。影片提到，Sonnet 的價格較前代降低約兩成、生成速度提升約三成，另有速度更快但費用加倍的模式；在 Aider 等評測中，Sonnet 的高效能模式可用較低成本達到 Opus 高階模式的水準，而最高模式則刷新多項紀錄。

更具體的實例來自與電路板設計公司 Dynomite 的合作：模型只收到一項任務，就獨立設計家用語音助理、USB 發電器與桌上電子寵物。它撰寫規格、挑選零件、安排 249 個元件、完成多層電路佈線、製作 CAD 外殼並撰寫韌體。遇到內建佈線工具太慢時，模型還自行編寫自動佈線器；為避免喇叭耗電過高，也設計了音量提高時同步調暗 LED 燈環的節電機制。原型送製後，第三代裝置首次通電便成功運作。相關測試也顯示，新模型在電路佈局與 CAD 評測上大幅進步。

物理、化學與營運研究的突破

在理論物理方面，影片介紹模型處理兩個長年未解的問題：它完成了關於微型宇宙中黑洞是否會形成的龐大計算，並以兩種獨立方法交叉驗證；此外，它還算出量子重力研究中一項長期無法精確求得的數值，並整理成 131 頁論文。相關研究者坦言，對部分成果仍未能完全理解。

在化學實驗中，模型被隔離於文獻與資料庫之外，只能依靠分子結構圖與本地程式工具，推導複雜分子的合成路徑。三位頂尖生化學者盲測後，一致認為其成果達到合成化學博士生的水準。營運研究方面，代理團隊一次處理 203 個多年未解的最佳化問題，在 72 題刷新紀錄、45 題達到數學上的最優解；其中一項列車發車排程，在兩小時內提出更有效率且附有嚴謹證明的方案。

生物、資安與軟體工程

模型也將多種工具整合，用來預測基因療法常用 AAV 病毒衣殼的複雜蛋白組裝結構，測試 34 種衣殼後成功建模 28 種。資安方面，Claude 3.5 Sonnet 找出部分其他模型未能發現的漏洞，在 Anthropic 的內部測試中也優於先前版本；Mozilla 則運用它打造 Firefox 漏洞探索系統，取得顯著提升。

大飛接著指出，Anthropic 表示，其核心程式碼中超過九成已合併的改動，是 Claude 在人類指導下完成。另有團隊使用 Sonnet 將重要服務由 Python 遷移至 Rust，讓啟動速度提升約 26%。更令人驚訝的是，一名工程師只提供空資料夾並要求製作作業系統原型，模型便協調上千個子代理，連續工作八天，完成可在筆電啟動的系統，包含核心、驅動程式、檔案儲存、視窗介面與安裝程式等功能。

機器人控制與「鋸齒狀 AGI」

在機器人控制測試中，Claude 3.5 Sonnet 的得分高於前代模型。官方展示中，它能操控實體機器人轉開瓶蓋、解魔術方塊與畫圖；面對真實魔術方塊時，模型只根據六張照片便提出步驟精簡的解法，並未照搬一般人熟悉的解題順序。

最後，大飛引用賓夕法尼亞大學華頓商學院教授 Ethan Mollick 的觀察。Mollick 認為，模型幾乎已接近通用人工智慧，但更適合稱為「鋸齒狀 AGI」：能力分布並不平均，有些領域已遠超人類預期，另一些方面仍明顯落後。影片因此呈現出新模型驚人的跨領域成果，也提醒觀眾不應把單項突破誤認為所有能力都已成熟。
